The overall architecture of SIR-Agent is shown in Fig. 2 (a).
Given a degraded image, the SIR-Agent progressively loads relevant skills from the skill library.
The initial skill library is constructed from restoration trajectories, as detailed in Sec. 4.1 .
Each skill specifies applicability conditions, ordered operations, and tool configurations.
Once candidate skills are collected, the MLLM selects the skill whose applicability conditions match the observed degradations.
The SIR-Agent invokes the configured tools in the specified order to obtain the restored image.
The restoration trajectory provides CFSR with intermediate images, tool calls, configurations, and feedback to revise the selected skill.

Restoration skills enable strategy reuse but may become ineffective when degradation conditions change.
Relying only on the final restored image makes it difficult to identify which operation needs revision, because the image reflects the combined effects of all operations.
Therefore, we propose Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR), which uses restoration-chain feedback to guide targeted skill revision.
As shown in Fig. 2 (b), CFSR comprises patched skill generation, patched skill validation, and skill updates.
Patched skill generation takes a skill s s and its restoration trajectory as inputs.
The MLLM examines intermediate images and chain feedback to identify suspicious steps.
Localization considers residual degradations and the effects of each operation on subsequent steps.
Using the restoration trajectory and identified operations, CFSR retrieves the top- K K candidate tools through LlamaIndex [ 25 ] .
For each identified operation, CFSR tests candidate tools on the same intermediate input image and compares the restoration quality of their outputs.
The best-performing tool is selected for each operation, and the selected replacements form a patched skill s ′ s^{\prime} .
The patched skill updates the associated tool configurations while retaining the operation order.

During patched skill validation, CFSR applies s ′ s^{\prime} to historical degraded images { u n } n = 1 N \{u_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} associated with s s .
The new restored images are compared with the corresponding old restored images obtained using s s .
Following the metric set used in [ 43 ] , we evaluate the old and new restored images with CLIP-IQA [ 42 ] , HyperIQA [ 38 ] , NIQE [ 29 ] , CPBD [ 31 ] , BRISQUE [ 28 ] , MUSIQ [ 18 ] , and LIQE [ 60 ] .
To combine the metric scores, we normalize them to a common scale, with NIQE [ 29 ] and BRISQUE [ 28 ] reversed so that higher values consistently indicate better quality.
The normalized scores are then aggregated into a single quality score Q Q .
For each historical input u n u_{n} , F s ​ ( u n ) F_{s}(u_{n}) and F s ′ ​ ( u n ) F_{s^{\prime}}(u_{n}) denote the old and new restored images, respectively.
The per-image quality change is:

Δ ​ Q ¯ = 1 N ∑ n = 1 N Δ Q n , R reg = 1 N ∑ n = 1 N 𝟏 [ Δ Q n < − ϵ ] , \overline{\Delta Q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Delta Q_{n},\qquad R_{\mathrm{reg}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[\Delta Q_{n}<-\epsilon], (2) where ϵ ≥ 0 \epsilon\geq 0 is a tolerance for small quality fluctuations and 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. Δ ​ Q ¯ \overline{\Delta Q} measures the overall benefit, while R reg R_{\mathrm{reg}} captures losses on individual prior cases.
However, a positive Δ ​ Q ¯ \overline{\Delta Q} can hide regressions on individual inputs.
Therefore, a patched skill is compatible when Δ ​ Q ¯ > 0 \overline{\Delta Q}>0 and R reg ≤ τ R_{\mathrm{reg}}\leq\tau , where τ \tau is the permitted regression rate.
A compatible patch updates the original skill; otherwise, the original skill is retained and the patched skill is added as a new entry with its inferred applicability conditions.
CFSR records revision decisions, tool trials, replay outcomes, library updates, and resource usage in a revision trajectory, which RSI-driven skill meta-learning analyzes to improve CFSR’s revision rules.

Fixed revision rules cannot incorporate lessons from earlier revisions, so CFSR may repeat ineffective edits and redundant tool trials on similar cases.
Inspired by RSI [ 47 ] , we design a skill meta-learning mechanism that improves CFSR’s external revision instructions using recorded trajectories, as illustrated in Fig. 3 .
The MLLM examines the trajectories to connect inefficient revision steps with the instructions that guide them.
For example, repeated edits without quality gains motivate changes to step priorities.
Low-yield trials motivate adjustments to tool retrieval and ranking, while stalled search guides changes to candidate expansion, operation switching, or stopping.
The resulting proposals target external revision rules, including those for step localization, tool selection, and revision control.
To evaluate the proposals, CFSR is run with the current and candidate rules on the same validation cases and starting skills, using the same tool library and budget limits.
Restoration gain is the mean Q Q improvement over the starting skills; revision cost is measured by actual tool calls and MLLM token usage.
At round t t , the next CFSR rule set is selected from the current set ℛ t cur \mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cur}} and the candidate set ℛ t cand \mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}} proposed by the MLLM: ℛ t + 1 cur = { ℛ t cand , ℛ t cand ∈ ℱ t , ℛ t cand ≻ ℛ t cur , ℛ t cur , otherwise , \mathcal{R}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{cur}}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}},&\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}}\in\mathcal{F}_{t},\;\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}}\succ\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cur}},\\
\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{cur}},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (3) where ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} denotes the candidate rule sets that meet the predefined requirement for preserving prior-task performance after skill revision.
The relation ≻ \succ gives priority to higher restoration gain, with lower revision cost preferred when gains are comparable.
Equation 3 adopts the candidate rules only when both conditions hold; otherwise, the current rules are retained.
Section 3.2 decides how to update individual skills, while Eq. 3 selects the rules that guide subsequent revisions.
Accepted rules guide subsequent CFSR runs, whose revision trajectories provide feedback for the next rule update.
The recursive feedback refines the revision procedure itself, aiming to reduce repeated ineffective edits and unnecessary tool trials.

evidence.quote: Our objective is to push capability boundaries and improve performance on subsequent tasks through continuous updates to the external harness, without modifying parameters θ \theta . During evaluation, the harness state H t H_{t} is strictly frozen, and test feedback is excluded from evolution.

For each selected resource, the system retrieves code, prepares the runtime environment, and constructs a callable interface. For tools based on pretrained models, it also automatically downloads and deploys the required weights. We represent each deployed candidate tool u ∈ 𝒰 t u\in\mathcal{U}_{t} as: u = ( r , ω , ℰ , g ) , u=(r,\omega,\mathcal{E},g), (5) where r r denotes the retrieved implementation, ω \omega represents the pretrained weights, ℰ \mathcal{E} signifies the runtime environment, and g g stands for the interface. The interface is responsible for receiving task data and operational parameters, invoking the underlying implementation, and returning results. For tools that do not rely on pretrained models, we set ω = ∅ \omega=\varnothing .

Each candidate tool u ∈ 𝒰 t u\in\mathcal{U}_{t} undergoes an execution check. If an invocation fails, the system uses the returned error information to revise the interface adapter code and repeats the check. Let 𝒱 exec ​ ( u ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{exec}}(u)\in\{0,1\} denote the final execution check outcome. The set of accepted tools is: 𝒰 t pass = { u ∈ 𝒰 t ∣ 𝒱 exec ​ ( u ) = 1 } . \mathcal{U}_{t}^{\mathrm{pass}}=\left\{u\in\mathcal{U}_{t}\mid\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{exec}}(u)=1\right\}. (6) Tools that pass the execution check are registered in the toolset, yielding the updated available toolset: 𝒯 ~ t = 𝒯 t ∪ 𝒰 t pass . \widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{t}\cup\mathcal{U}_{t}^{\mathrm{pass}}. (7) The newly registered specialized tools are immediately available to support the current task’s execution, enabling the dynamic adaptation of the workflow, and persistently retained for reuse in subsequent tasks.

Given a task z t z_{t} , the system retrieves a set of relevant skills 𝒦 t \mathcal{K}_{t} from the current skill library 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} : 𝒦 t = Retrieve θ ⁡ ( z t , 𝒮 t ) . \mathcal{K}_{t}=\operatorname{Retrieve}_{\theta}(z_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t}). (8) The planner would read these documents and combines their structured guidance with the current remote sensing data and task requirements to construct and dynamically adapt the initial execution workflow: W t ( 0 ) = Plan θ ⁡ ( z t , 𝒯 t , 𝒦 t ) , W_{t}^{(0)}=\operatorname{Plan}_{\theta}(z_{t};\mathcal{T}_{t},\mathcal{K}_{t}), (9) where 𝒯 t \mathcal{T}_{t} denotes the toolset currently available during the initial planning phase. The retrieved skills guide the selection of processing steps and parameters. If no applicable skill is found, we set 𝒦 t = ∅ \mathcal{K}_{t}=\varnothing , and the planner directly generates a workflow from the task requirements and the existing toolset. If tool evolution is triggered during execution, the system leverages the newly acquired tools to dynamically adapt and finalize the workflow into W t W_{t} .

After task completion, the system performs a closed-loop update of the skill library using the final workflow W t W_{t} , execution trace τ t \tau_{t} , and task feedback f t f_{t} . Verified successful workflows are distilled into new skills by the base model θ \theta . Concurrently, existing skills are revised, merged, or deactivated based on their historical reuse outcomes, which are tracked as success rates and invocation counts. Deactivated skills will no longer participate in subsequent planning stages. This update process can be expressed as: 𝒮 t + 1 = Update θ ⁡ ( 𝒮 t , W t , z t , τ t , f t ) . \mathcal{S}_{t+1}=\operatorname{Update}_{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_{t},W_{t},z_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}). (10) If newly acquired tools are invoked in a successful workflow, their complete usage procedures are also retained within the generated skill documents, thereby directly supporting future workflow planning through retrieval.

Datasets. We evaluate RemoteEvolver on Earth-Bench [ 5 ] and OpenEarthAgent-Bench [ 18 ] . We split tasks into evolution and test sets at a ratio of 7:3. When splitting, we aim to keep task category distribution similar in both sets.

As shown in Fig. 3 , while the overall accuracy initially rises, subsequent checkpoints reveal a non-monotonic trend. Specifically, while near-domain transfer FWT Near \mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Near}} remains largely positive, far-domain transfer FWT Far \mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Far}} suffers from severe fluctuations, sometimes dropping below 0 on OpenEarthAgent-Bench. Simultaneously, the retention rate abnormally increases, indicating the agent forgets previously mastered tasks. These observations highlight a critical insight: simply expanding the harness does not guarantee stable performance growth . Thus, we conduct a deep analysis and attribute this non-monotonic degradation to a cascading effect across three levels of the agent’s expanded action space: tool exploration, skill retrieval, and workflow execution, as illustrated in Appendix.

Coupled to the simulator and likelihood,
the agent writes an inference algorithm, tests it on sim-
ulated observations, reads from the weights why it fails,
and rewrites its coordinates, symmetries, and factoriza-
tion until it passes the weight check and a calibration test
with known parameters on held-out simulations. The re-
sult is an amortized algorithm for that field in which a
network trained once on simulations (one per planetary
system for orbits), combined where needed with a local
coordinate chart fitted to the observation, proposes the
posterior of any new observation and the exact likelihood
reweights and checks it.
